panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Sagittal T1w cranial MRI of the same 5-year-old child with enzymatically and HEXA-molecularly confirmed infantile-onset Tay-Sachs disease. Shows cerebral cortical and cerebellar atrophy with wide sulci/shrunken gyri and reduced T1w white-matter intensity (demyelination), plus abnormal deep gray matter (basal ganglia) signal. Real human patient radiology of the target disease; panels are unlabeled in the source and are assigned left-to-right. [raw subtype: infantile-onset] B: Coronal T2w cranial MRI of the same confirmed infantile-onset Tay-Sachs patient. Visibly demonstrates diffuse T2-hyperintense white matter disease (demyelination), cerebral cortical and cerebellar atrophy, and abnormal bilateral deep gray matter (basal ganglia/thalamic) signal. Real human patient image of the target disease. [raw subtype: infantile-onset] C: Axial T2w FLAIR cranial MRI of the same confirmed infantile-onset Tay-Sachs patient. Shows diffuse...
panels.attribution_text: Cox. Lysosomal Diseases and Neuropsychiatry: Opportunities to Rebalance the Mind.. Frontiers in molecular biosciences 2020. doi:10.3389/fmolb.2020.00177. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Cranial imaging in a 5 year-old child with infantile-onset GM2 gangliosidosis. Magnetic resonance images (left to right: sagittal T1w; coronal T2w; axial T2w FLAIR). Note the cerebral cortical and cerebellar atrophy with wide sulci and shrunken gyri; there are symmetrical diffuse white matter changes with reduced T1w intensity and hyper-intense signals in T2w images – the latter indicating demyelination. Abnormal signal intensity is seen in basal ganglia, peducles, and brain stem. Female infant born after normal delivery to unrelated white British parents without Ashkenazi ancestry; hypotonia noted at 7 months with cherry-red spots observed. Tay-Sachs disease confirmed enzymatically and by molecular analysis of the HEXA gene (well-known “severe” mutation frequent in British “Celtic” patients was identified). With scrupulous care and potentially salutary effects of a substrate-reducing agent (miglustat), the illness followed an unexpectedly protracted course. Nonetheless, characteristic startle responses to sounds, loss of motor skills, epilepsy and episodes of aspiration pneumonia led to deterioration with a peaceful death, aged 8 years.
in_text_mentions: Figures 1, 2 extensive neurological injury involving nearly every neuron in a florid pathological process: at least 10% of the dry weight of the enlarged brain of infants dying of Tay-Sachs disease is due to the sialylated sphingolipid, GM2 ganglioside (normal, < 0.1%).

panels.rationale: Bilateral fundus photographs showing cherry-red spots in the maculae of a 1.5-year-old child, with Tay-Sachs disease confirmed by β-hexosaminidase A enzyme deficiency. The cherry-red spot is the classic textbook ophthalmic manifestation of Tay-Sachs disease (GM2 gangliosidosis). The image is a real patient fundus photograph with clear diagnostic quality, directly attributed to Tay-Sachs disease by both the caption and in-text evidence.

panels.rationale: Color fundus photograph of the right eye of a child with Tay-Sachs disease (article title: 'Choroidal coloboma in a case of tay-sachs disease'). The in-text explicitly states a cherry red spot was noted in both eyes and that the rest of the right-eye fundus was normal (Figure 3); the image shows the optic disc and a pale macular area with a central red spot, the classic cherry-red spot of Tay-Sachs disease. Real patient image, clear manifestation, classic presentation.
panels.attribution_text: Ahmed et al. Choroidal coloboma in a case of tay-sachs disease.. Case reports in ophthalmological medicine 2014. doi:10.1155/2014/760746. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
in_text_mentions: On ocular examination, pupils were reactive to light. The child did not fixate or follow light. The anterior segment in the right eye was within normal limits. In the left eye a typical iris coloboma was appreciated in the inferonasal quadrant (Figure 2). The lens in both eyes was transparent. A cherry red spot was noted in both eyes. Rest of the fundus was normal in the right eye (Figure 3). Left eye showed type III choroidal coloboma by Ida Mann's classification (Figure 4). No disc pallor was noted.

panels.rationale: Color fundus photograph of the left eye of a child with Tay-Sachs disease. The disease-focused article title ('Choroidal coloboma in a case of tay-sachs disease') together with the specific in-text captioned manifestation ('Left eye showed type III choroidal coloboma by Ida Mann's classification (Figure 4)') supports attribution to Tay-Sachs disease. The image visibly shows a large pale/white area of absent choroid inferior to the disc consistent with choroidal coloboma, plus a central dark spot; the in-text also documents a cherry-red spot in both eyes. Choroidal coloboma is an unusual association with Tay-Sachs rather than a classic manifestation, so typicality is atypical and confidence is moderate. The choroidal coloboma finding is not in the allowed vocabulary and is therefore proposed.
panels.attribution_text: Ahmed et al. Choroidal coloboma in a case of tay-sachs disease.. Case reports in ophthalmological medicine 2014. doi:10.1155/2014/760746. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
in_text_mentions: On ocular examination, pupils were reactive to light. The child did not fixate or follow light. The anterior segment in the right eye was within normal limits. In the left eye a typical iris coloboma was appreciated in the inferonasal quadrant (Figure 2). The lens in both eyes was transparent. A cherry red spot was noted in both eyes. Rest of the fundus was normal in the right eye (Figure 3). Left eye showed type III choroidal coloboma by Ida Mann's classification (Figure 4). No disc pallor was noted.
